subject: Fit a normal curve with inlabru?

messages.author: 891cbebc640d4273
messages.subject: Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
parts:
Hi!

Having successfully fitted some nonlinear models with inlabru, I'm testing to see if I  can use it to fit a normal distribution curve to data. So far without success - it doesn't seem able to estimate the sd. Here's some example code:

library(data.table)
meand=0    #Mean of the curve
sdd=1      #sd of the curve
h=1        #height of the peak
x=seq(-10,10,length=1000)
varsamp=0.01          #error variance
precision=1/varsamp
sdsamp=sqrt(varsamp)

inputdt=data.table(expand.grid(x=x,ind=seq(1:10)))
inputdt[,indref:=paste("I",x,ind,sep="_")]
inputdt[,h:=h]
inputdt[,meand:=meand]
inputdt[,sdd:=sdd]

#data points including error variance.
inputdt[,normcurve:=h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2))) + rnorm(.N,0,sdsamp)]

plot(normcurve~x,data=inputdt)
points((h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2))))~x,data=inputdt,col="red",pch=16,cex=0.3)

#Likelihood model.
  lik <- inlabru::like(
    family = "gaussian", data = inputdt,
    formula = normcurve~h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*sdd^2)))
  )

#This doesn't work.
fita <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) + sdd(1) - 1, lik)
summary(fita)

#This works.
fita2 <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) - 1, lik)
summary(fita2)

I know I can use other packages for this, I'm actually fitting a more complex model, which also works well if I don't try to estimate the sdd parameter.

Is there a way to fit this model?

Thanks, Richard.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
parts:
Hi,

it's an initial value issue; The default starting point for the
linearisation is all latent variables being zero. In your
parameterisation, there's no way to "escape" from that point.
You can set initial values for the two problematic parameters h and sdd with
options = list(bru_initial = list(h = 2, sdd = 2))

However, that's not quite enough, as the parameterisation doesn't have
a unique solution for sdd; the predictor isn't monotonic in sdd.
But this is easily fixed here, since you can use a log-transformation
for the sdd parameterisation, with exp(log_sdd) instead of sdd.
The following works:

lik <- inlabru::like(
family = "gaussian", data = inputdt,

formula = normcurve~h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2)))
)
fita <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) + log_sdd(1) - 1, lik,
options = list(bru_initial = list(h = 2)))

> fita$summary.fixed
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant
0.975quant mode kld
h 1.010092214 0.004245507 1.001768795 1.010092215
1.018415635 NA 5.543583e-11
meand 0.001966013 0.004772272 -0.007390147 0.001966014
0.011322175 NA 5.353491e-11
log_sdd -0.010752056 0.004821584 -0.020204893 -0.010752055
-0.001299217 NA 5.352113e-11
> exp(fita$summary.fixed["log_sdd", c("0.025quant", "0.5quant", "0.975quant")])
0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant
log_sdd 0.9799979 0.9893055 0.9987016

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
parts:
Hi list,

Just picking up this discussion again, with a new query regarding fitting nonlinear curves with inlabru - specifically how to fit curves to binary data. I'm fitting several different curves, including the normal curve described in the earlier posts (and see code below), to continuous data with normally distributed errors, and would like to also fit these curves to binary response data. So my general question is, how to set up 'lik' and 'bru' for nonlinear curves when response data are non-gaussian?

As a separate question, I'd also like to learn how to specify priors for these parameters. Can someone point me to example code for setting the priors in inlabru please, or how to find the help files?

The code below creates both gaussian and binary data (coded 0,1) using the same 'normal' function, and then fits the gaussian data, but not the binary data.

###
library(data.table)
###

# For simplicity, I'm fitting the curve to a set of samples collected along a 1D linear transect. I'm hoping to get into more complicated stuff later.

#1000 sample sites along a linear transect, with 10 sampled individuals per site.
Nsites=1000
Nindpersite=10

meand=0                                   #Mean of the curve
sdd=1                                        #sd of the curve
h=1                                            #height of the peak
x=seq(-10,10,length=Nsites)

varsamp=0.01                        #error variance
precision=1/varsamp
sdsamp=sqrt(varsamp)
inputdt=data.table(expand.grid(x=x,ind=seq(1:Nindpersite)))

inputdt[,indref:=paste("I",x,ind,sep="_")]
inputdt[,h:=h]
inputdt[,meand:=meand]
inputdt[,sdd:=sdd]

inputdt[,log_sdd:=log(sdd)]            #The value I'm estimating#

#data with gaussian errors.
inputdt[,normcurve:=h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2))) + rnorm(.N,0,sdsamp)]


#Now making some binary data.

inputdt[,binarydat:=rbinom(.N,1,prob=
 h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2)))
                          )]

#The blue line in the plot below is a smooth.spline fitted through the binary data (not plotted).

plot(normcurve~x,data=inputdt,pch=16,cex=0.3,col="grey")                                                                  #The gaussian data#
points((h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2))))~x,data=inputdt,col="red",pch=16,cex=0.3)   #The 'true' curve#
lines(smooth.spline(inputdt$binarydat~inputdt$x),col="blue")                                                             #spline fitted to binary data#

#Model fitting for the gaussian data, which works well.

lik <- inlabru::like(
  family = "gaussian", data = inputdt,
  formula = normcurve~h*exp(-((x - meand)^2/(2*exp(log_sdd)^2)))
)

fita <- bru(~ h(1) + meand(1) + log_sdd(1) - 1, lik,

options = list(bru_initial = list(h = 2)))                  #I actually ran it successfully without setting bru_initial; h can potentially be 0 or negative#


What would be the equivalent 'lik' and 'bru' for the binary data? Is there a general rule for non-gaussian data? 

(Separate question) How do I specify the priors?

Many thanks and best wishes,
Richard.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit a normal curve with inlabru?
parts:
Hi Richard,
this would probably be easier to answer if you post is as a question
at https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlabru/discussions
to make it easier to read&comment on the code.

For prior specifications, it works as in plain INLA, which is that
components with fixed effects take arguments mean.linear and
prec.linear, and for hyperparameters for structured random effect
components,
hyper = list(...)
In your example, you only have "fixed effect" type parameters, so use
mean.linear and prec.linear to specify their N(m,prec^(-1) ) priors.

For non-gaussian priors for those, you need to build that into the
transformations (e.g. you now have exp(log_sdd) for the std.dev.
parameter, giving a log-normal prior on that.
For an exponential prior, you would need the effect of
qexp(pnorm(internal_sdd), rate = prior_rate) where internal_rate is
given a N(0,1) prior.
I can answer more on the inlabru/discussions pages (we have some new
helper functions for such transformations)

Finn

>

>

>

> Richard.

>> this would probably be easier to answer if you post is as a question
>> at https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlabru/discussions
>> to make it easier to read&comment on the code.
>>
>> For prior specifications, it works as in plain INLA, which is that
>> components with fixed effects take arguments mean.linear and
>> prec.linear, and for hyperparameters for structured random effect
>> components,
>> hyper = list(...)
>> In your example, you only have "fixed effect" type parameters, so use
>> mean.linear and prec.linear to specify their N(m,prec^(-1) ) priors.
>>
>> For non-gaussian priors for those, you need to build that into the
>> transformations (e.g. you now have exp(log_sdd) for the std.dev.
>> parameter, giving a log-normal prior on that.
>> For an exponential prior, you would need the effect of
>> qexp(pnorm(internal_sdd), rate = prior_rate) where internal_rate is
>> given a N(0,1) prior.
>> I can answer more on the inlabru/discussions pages (we have some new
>> helper functions for such transformations)
>>
>> Finn
